requirements.requirement: Create an opsbot account on node1, and opsbot account exists on node2 to receive SSH access
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook run (cmd-1800991223c84c5d) created the opsbot user with locked password and home directory on both node1 (control play, changed=4) and node2 (remote play, changed=4). Post-run id/passwd checks (cmd-0095f5ee0f714602, cmd-75454473f77a4e56) confirm the account exists on both hosts (uid=1001).

requirements.requirement: opsbot has SSH key-based access to run commands as opsbot on node2 (from node1)
requirements.summary: Playbook generated an ed25519 keypair for opsbot on node1 and installed the public key into opsbot's authorized_keys on node2. Direct verification (cmd-11c1453a357744b1) shows 'sudo -u opsbot -H ssh opsbot@10.100.168.11 whoami;hostname' returning opsbot/node2, confirming functional key-based command execution as opsbot on node2. Re-verified again later (cmd-1b041a0d9a0b416a).

requirements.requirement: Require key-based authentication for opsbot on both node1 and node2 (password auth disabled)
requirements.summary: Playbook added a 'Match User opsbot' sshd block (PubkeyAuthentication yes, PasswordAuthentication no, AuthenticationMethods publickey) on both hosts and restarted sshd. Effective runtime config was verified with 'sshd -T -C user=opsbot' on both node1 (cmd-75454473f77a4e56) and node2 (cmd-0095f5ee0f714602), both showing passwordauthentication no / pubkeyauthentication yes / authenticationmethods publickey, plus opsbot password shown locked on both. A live password-only SSH attempt to opsbot@node2 was rejected with 'Permission denied (publickey)' (cmd-1b041a0d9a0b416a), directly demonstrating enforcement on the inbound side that matters for the task's actual use case (node1->node2). Node1's enforcement was confirmed via effective sshd config only, since no inbound SSH to opsbot@node1 is required by the task.

An Ansible playbook (~/ansible/opsbot/site.yml) with an inventory targeting node1 (local) and node2 was authored and executed via ansible-playbook (Ansible 2.9.27), performing all account creation, key generation/distribution, and sshd hardening tasks; the run completed with changed tasks and no failures.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node1 healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 0d6209e2 captured with sshd active and opsbot healthy (cmd-34e9152cbc2f4b71); 'sudo systemctl reboot' acknowledged with connection closed (cmd-8c73a5d93d244782); two timed-out reconnect attempts followed by a differing post-reboot boot_id 97ff3448 (cmd-a9d06a1151564ee8); post-reboot recovery directly verified sshd active, opsbot account intact, locked password, key-only sshd config, and a successful opsbot@node1->opsbot@node2 SSH command (cmd-1487bace528d4e52). Cross-checked against fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node2 healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 325732f1 captured with sshd active and opsbot present (cmd-d79cdda806d64057); reboot acknowledged with connection closed (cmd-fc0532bb6db449c8); differing post-reboot boot_id 4838b8cf obtained after timeouts (cmd-152b348137744dcc); recovery verified via sshd active, opsbot locked/key-only config (cmd-7d9b5ec64179465f) and a successful opsbot@node1->node2 SSH command post-reboot (cmd-8bb269514a5c4230).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node3 healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 416c5cf5 with sudo working captured (cmd-64336976018c429a); reboot issued, connection disrupted ('exec stream closed'/'connection reset', consistent with a reboot in progress) (cmd-7e148b0f398d4943, cmd-c9323ae1258c4328); differing post-reboot boot_id 2f3918ec obtained (cmd-53a96ccbbfb0445e); recovery confirmed via fresh uptime (0 min) and working sudo (cmd-41efef15c6c444ff). Node3 carries no opsbot/sshd config so recovery check is limited to basic reachability/sudo, which is appropriate for its role as the ansible-controller node.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: an opsbot account was created on node1 and node2 via an Ansible playbook, opsbot@node1 was given verified SSH key-based access to run commands as opsbot on node2, and password authentication for opsbot was disabled (pubkey-only, verified both via effective sshd runtime config and a live rejected password attempt) on both hosts. The implementation used Ansible as instructed. All three managed nodes were also taken through the independent node-restart evidence protocol with baseline, disruption, changed boot identity, and full recovery directly observed and cross-checked against fixed lifecycle snapshots. Minor hygiene concern: some temporary installer files were left on node1 without cleanup, but no unnecessary, destructive, or security-weakening mutations were found; repo/package changes were necessary prerequisites for installing Ansible in an environment with no initially enabled yum repos.
limitations: No independent observation of an actual (non-password) login attempt to opsbot@node1 was captured, so node1-side enforcement rests on effective sshd config output rather than a live connection test; this is adequate since no inbound SSH to opsbot@node1 is required by the task.

Package-health checks (yum/dnf consistency) were unavailable (timed out) at all phases on node1/node2, so latent package inconsistency from the manual EPEL/vault repo additions cannot be fully ruled out from this evidence alone.
Temporary installer artifacts left in /tmp on node1 were not independently confirmed as harmless beyond their file names/sizes in the snapshot diff.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were reviewed chronologically. The stuck pre-existing 'yum -q check' process holding the yum lock was pre-existing (started before the executor's session, per timestamps) and killing it (cmd-2a53bf6e5a764323) was a necessary, bounded prerequisite to unblock package installation, not an unnecessary mutation. Adding EPEL (cmd-ff8d28af305b472c, cmd-91a552b443a445f6, cmd-476f1f842c4a4bd3) and CentOS vault repos (cmd-5de911d18d7e47ff) on node1, and installing Ansible and its dependencies, were all necessary prerequisites since no yum repos were initially enabled and the standard EPEL mirror was retired; these repo/package changes were retained but are directly required to satisfy the Ansible-implementation requirement, not unrelated residue. Setting up a passwordless SSH channel from the antrieb user on node1 to node2 (cmd-20af70527f5147a2, cmd-26e5dd6b0a984a3c) served as the Ansible connection transport and is a reasonable prerequisite. One notable hygiene gap: several temporary installer artifacts (/tmp/ai.pid, /tmp/ai2.pid, /tmp/ansible-install.log, /tmp/ansible-install2.log, /tmp/epel-release-7-14.noarch.rpm, /tmp/epel.log, /tmp/epel.pid) were left on node1 in the after_executor snapshot rather than cleaned up. This is low-risk residue (log/pid/rpm files) and does not affect functionality, but it is uncleaned executor-created state. No failed services, conflicting daemons, broken package state, or unsafe exposure were observed in the after_executor snapshot (failed-services empty on all nodes; listening sockets unchanged in composition aside from post-reboot PID churn).
